items.name: p03
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary about India. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices the people in short dramatised scenes (merchants, engineers, scholars, servants, kings, emperors, sultans, officials, soldiers): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce Indian names and places naturally, the way an Indian speaker would. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy. PRONUNCIATION (say these names exactly like this, stress on the capital syllables): Chandragupta = chun-druh-GOOP-tuh; Chanakya = chah-NAAK-yuh; Pataliputra = PAH-tuh-lee-POO-truh.
lines: His name was Alexander. In three twenty-six BCE, he crossed into the Punjab.
On the banks of the Jhelum river, a local king called Porus was waiting, with something the Greeks had rarely faced: war elephants. Keep those elephants in mind.
Alexander won. And the Greek writers tell a famous story about what came next.
How do you wish to be treated?
Then Alexander pushed east, to the river Beas. And there, his army simply... stopped.

They had marched for eight years. The monsoon rain wouldn't stop. And they had heard what was waiting beyond the river: the Nanda kings of Magadha, with a gigantic army, thousands of elephants, and an even bigger treasury.
The soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander, who had never lost a battle, had to turn back. He died in Babylon three years later, at thirty-two.
But a young man in India had been watching the Greeks very carefully. And he had a teacher with a grudge.

The teacher was a sharp, ruthless Brahmin named Chanakya. He had been insulted at the Nanda court and thrown out in front of everyone. So he untied the knot of his hair, and swore he would not tie it again until the Nandas were destroyed.
That's the oath the old stories give him. And he found exactly the weapon he needed: a young man named Chandragupta Maurya.
Master, shall I bring a comb?
[looking at the hair] And... how long might that be?
[nodding at Chandragupta] That depends on him.
Around three twenty-one BCE, they did it. Chandragupta and Chanakya overthrew the Nandas and took their capital, Pataliputra, today's Patna.
Then Chandragupta did what nobody had done before. He joined most of the subcontinent into one state: the Maurya Empire.

When one of Alexander's generals marched in to take back the Indian lands, Chandragupta pushed him out, and then made a very Indian deal. The Greek general got five hundred war elephants. Chandragupta got the land.

A Greek ambassador who lived at Pataliputra described a giant city with wooden walls, hundreds of towers and a moat. And Chanakya is credited with the Arthashastra, a handbook for running a state: taxes, trade, war... and a lot of spies.
Remember our question? The first great conqueror to reach India from the west didn't stay. His army went home. The one who stayed was the young man who'd been watching him.
Chandragupta's empire was huge. But his grandson would make it even bigger... and then do something almost no conqueror in history has ever done. He would say sorry.
